content: Fractures of the tibial plateau, which involve the knee joint and are intra-articular in nature, present significant challenges in treatment due to their complexity and high rates of complications, including early-onset osteoarthritis. Surgical fixation is typically employed for more severe or complex tibial plateau fractures. Additionally, bone void fillers are frequently utilized to address bone defects resulting from the injury. However, there is currently no consensus on the optimal surgical fixation method or the most effective bone void filler. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of various surgical interventions and the use of bone void fillers in the treatment of tibial plateau fractures. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled clinical trials that compared different surgical techniques and types of bone void fillers. Six trials involving 429 adult participants, predominantly male (63%), were included. These trials were small in scale and carried a substantial risk of bias, leading to very low-quality evidence overall. One trial compared hybrid fixation, which combines a circular fixator with percutaneous screws, to standard open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) in patients with Schatzker types V or VI tibial plateau fractures. Quality of life scores, including the 36-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) scores, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) function scores, tended to favor hybrid fixation. However, the possibility of ORIF being equally beneficial could not be excluded. Participants in the hybrid fixation group had a lower risk of unplanned reoperation (351 per 1000 people compared to 450 per 1000 in the ORIF group) and were more likely to return to their pre-injury activity level (303 per 1000 people compared to 121 per 1000 in the ORIF group). Both groups showed comparable results for WOMAC pain and stiffness scores, but the hybrid fixation group demonstrated a greater range of knee motion. Another trial compared the use of a minimally invasive plate system (LISS) to double-plating ORIF in 84 patients with bicondylar tibial plateau fractures. Nearly twice as many participants in the ORIF group required a bone graft (22 versus 12). The trial did not report on quality of life, pain, knee range of motion, or return to pre-injury activity. There was no evidence of differences in HSS knee scores, complications, or reoperations requiring implant removal or revision fixation between the two groups. A quasi-randomized trial evaluated arthroscopically-assisted percutaneous reduction and internal fixation versus standard ORIF in 58 patients with Schatzker types II or III tibial plateau fractures. At 14 months, there was very low-quality evidence suggesting higher HSS knee scores and greater knee range of motion in the arthroscopically-assisted group. Quality of life, pain, and return to pre-injury activity were not reported, and no reoperations were documented. Three trials investigated the use of bone substitutes compared to autologous bone grafts (autografts) for managing bone defects. Quality of life, pain, and return to pre-injury activity were not reported in these trials. One trial with 25 participants reported good or excellent lower limb function outcomes in both groups at 12 months, including walking, climbing stairs, squatting, and jumping. The incidence of complications was similar between groups across all three trials. One trial reported no inflammatory responses in participants receiving bone substitutes, while two trials found no complications at the donor site in the autograft group. However, in one trial, all 38 participants who underwent autologous iliac bone grafting reported prolonged pain at the harvest site. Two trials reported similar knee range of motion outcomes between groups, while the third trial favored the bone substitute group. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine the best surgical fixation method or the most effective approach to addressing bone defects in tibial plateau fractures. However, the findings do not contradict strategies that aim to minimize soft-tissue dissection and damage or avoid complications associated with autograft donor sites by using bone substitutes. Further well-designed, larger randomized trials are necessary to provide more definitive guidance.
